_about: The world's events, shared by every story. One record per event: what happened, when, and where — checked once, used everywhere. A story picks the ones inside its span (js/timeline.js, `pool`), says which side of its line each one sits on, and may add `why`: the last sentence, in that story's voice, tying it to that picture. A story never rewrites these words. Places are ids from stories/places.json. Years are plain years; a fraction places an event inside its year (1815.3 is April). Spec: CWVault/claude/Story-Pattern.md.

leeuwenhoek-born-1632.label: Leeuwenhoek born
leeuwenhoek-born-1632.title: The boy who would see the invisible
leeuwenhoek-born-1632.text: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was baptised in the New Church at Delft four days after Johannes Vermeer. He grew up to make the best microscopes of his time, and to see tiny animals swimming in a drop of water.

night-watch-1642.label: Rembrandt paints The Night Watch
night-watch-1642.title: The Night Watch
night-watch-1642.text: Rembrandt’s biggest painting: a company of Amsterdam’s guards stepping out with their muskets and their banner, more than four metres wide.

galileo-dies-1642.label: Galileo dies
galileo-dies-1642.title: Galileo dies, and Newton is born
galileo-dies-1642.text: Galileo Galilei died in January 1642, in his house in the hills outside Florence. He had been one of the first to turn a telescope on the sky, and he saw mountains on the Moon. For saying that the Earth goes round the Sun, the Church had kept him shut up there for the last eight and a half years of his life. Isaac Newton was born the same year.

newton-born-1642.label: Newton born
newton-born-1642.title: Isaac Newton is born
newton-born-1642.text: On Christmas Day 1642, on a farm at Woolsthorpe in England. In the course of his lifetime he would work out the laws of motion, the law of gravity, and calculus.

ming-falls-1644.label: Chinese porcelain stops
ming-falls-1644.title: A war in China
ming-falls-1644.text: The Ming dynasty fell, and the blue-and-white porcelain the Dutch had been buying, much of it made in the kiln town of Jingdezhen, stopped coming.

delft-potteries-1647.label: Delft potters copy it
delft-potteries-1647.title: Four potteries, then twenty
delft-potteries-1647.text: Ordinary clay under a glaze made white with tin, painted with cobalt blue in Chinese patterns. Four potteries in 1647; more than twenty by 1661.

delft-thunderclap-1654.label: The gunpowder store explodes
delft-thunderclap-1654.title: The Delft Thunderclap
delft-thunderclap-1654.text: About forty thousand kilograms of gunpowder. More than two hundred houses flattened. The painter Carel Fabritius, who had studied with Rembrandt, died at his easel.

london-plague-1665.label: Plague in London
london-plague-1665.title: The Great Plague
london-plague-1665.text: Plague killed about a hundred thousand people in London, something like one in four. Cambridge University shut its doors, and a young Isaac Newton went home to the farm where he was born.

newton-prism-1666.label: Newton's prism
newton-prism-1666.title: White light is all the colours
newton-prism-1666.text: Newton was splitting sunlight into colours with a glass prism, and working out that white light is all of them at once.

bourgeois-gentleman-1670.label: Molière’s The Bourgeois Gentleman
bourgeois-gentleman-1670.title: Speaking prose all his life
bourgeois-gentleman-1670.text: Molière’s play was first performed for the King of France in October 1670, and then in Paris. In it Monsieur Jourdain is delighted to discover that he has been speaking prose all his life.

france-invades-1672.label: France invades
france-invades-1672.title: The disaster year
france-invades-1672.text: The armies of the King of France marched into the Republic and took Utrecht.

colour-prints-1765.label: The first full-colour prints
colour-prints-1765.title: Colour, block by block
colour-prints-1765.text: Suzuki Harunobu and his cutters worked out how to line up many blocks exactly, one for each colour. Before that a print was black lines with a wash or two.

meiwa-tsunami-1771.label: The Meiwa tsunami
meiwa-tsunami-1771.title: A wave that really came
meiwa-tsunami-1771.text: An earthquake sent a wave over the islands in the far south-west of Japan. In places it ran thirty metres up the hills, and about a third of the people living there were killed.

kaitai-shinsho-1774.label: A Dutch anatomy book in Japanese
kaitai-shinsho-1774.title: Kaitai Shinsho
kaitai-shinsho-1774.text: Three Japanese doctors watched a dissection with a Dutch anatomy book open beside them, saw that the Dutch book was right and their own books were wrong, and spent three years turning it into Japanese — though they could barely read Dutch. It came through the same door as the blue.

scheeles-green-1775.label: Scheele’s green
scheeles-green-1775.title: A beautiful green made of arsenic
scheeles-green-1775.text: Carl Wilhelm Scheele mixed copper with arsenic and got a green brighter than any other. It went into wallpaper, cloth, artificial flowers and, sometimes, sweets, and it went on quietly poisoning people for a hundred years.

elekiter-1776.label: Gennai’s electric machine
elekiter-1776.title: The elekiter
elekiter-1776.text: Hiraga Gennai repaired a broken Dutch machine that made sparks by rubbing glass, and showed it off in Edo. Fifty-five years later Faraday got electricity out of a magnet instead.

uranus-1781.label: Uranus is found
uranus-1781.title: A new planet
uranus-1781.text: William Herschel, looking through a telescope he had built himself, found a small green dot that moved. It was a planet, the first anybody had found since ancient times, and it put the edge of the Sun’s family twice as far out as it had been.

kokan-copperplate-1783.label: Shiba Kōkan’s copperplate
kokan-copperplate-1783.title: Depth on a flat sheet
kokan-copperplate-1783.text: Shiba Kōkan made the first copperplate etching in Japan, and took from Dutch books the trick of drawing things smaller as they go further away.

asama-tenmei-1783.label: Asama erupts; then the famine
asama-tenmei-1783.title: The sky dims and the rice fails
asama-tenmei-1783.text: The mountain buried the farms below it in ash, and a volcano in Iceland was erupting the same year. Cold summers followed, the rice failed again and again, and hundreds of thousands of people died in what is called the Tenmei famine. Thirty-two years later Tambora did the same thing on a bigger scale.

figaro-1786.label: Mozart’s Marriage of Figaro
figaro-1786.title: A servant outwits his master
figaro-1786.text: Mozart’s new opera opened in Vienna. It is about a servant who is cleverer than the count he works for, and it is still performed everywhere.

french-revolution-1789.label: The French Revolution begins
french-revolution-1789.title: The Bastille falls
french-revolution-1789.text: A crowd in Paris took the Bastille, the king’s prison, and France began pulling down its kings. Napoleon’s wars came out of it, and most of the dates in European history for the next thirty years.

red-chamber-1791.label: Dream of the Red Chamber is printed
red-chamber-1791.title: The great Chinese novel
red-chamber-1791.text: A long novel about a rich family’s rise and fall, written thirty years earlier and passed around in hand-made copies, was printed at last. Chinese readers have been arguing about its ending ever since.

phaeton-1808.label: A British warship forces its way in
phaeton-1808.title: The Phaeton
phaeton-1808.text: A British warship sailed into Nagasaki flying a Dutch flag, seized two Dutch traders, and would not leave until it was given food and water. Japan was humiliated, and it is one reason the door shut tighter.

tambora-1815.label: Tambora explodes
tambora-1815.title: The biggest eruption in recorded history
tambora-1815.text: The volcano Tambora, on an island in what is now Indonesia, blew apart in April 1815. Its ash went round the world, and the next year Europe and North America had no summer.

frankenstein-1816.label: Mary Shelley begins Frankenstein
frankenstein-1816.title: A summer with no summer in it
frankenstein-1816.text: The summer after Tambora was so cold and wet that a group of friends staying by Lake Geneva were kept indoors, and told each other ghost stories. One of them, Mary Shelley, who was eighteen, began Frankenstein.

kaleidoscope-1817.label: Brewster’s kaleidoscope
kaleidoscope-1817.title: Two mirrors in a tube
kaleidoscope-1817.text: David Brewster, a physicist in Edinburgh, patented the kaleidoscope: two mirrors in a tube, and loose bits of coloured glass at the end. Turn it and the pattern changes. It was copied so quickly that he made very little from it.

prussian-blue-japan-1820.label: Prussian blue in Japan, still dear
prussian-blue-japan-1820.title: A little of the Berlin blue
prussian-blue-japan-1820.text: Dutch ships had been bringing small amounts of the blue through Dejima for years. Painters used a little of it. It cost far too much for prints.

japan-drives-ships-1825.label: Japan orders foreign ships driven away
japan-drives-ships-1825.title: Drive them off
japan-drives-ships-1825.text: After more foreign ships came near the coast, the shogun’s government ordered that any of them be driven off, with cannon if need be.

cheap-prussian-blue-1829.label: Cheap Prussian blue arrives from China
cheap-prussian-blue-1829.title: The blue gets cheap
cheap-prussian-blue-1829.text: Chinese makers were now making the blue themselves, and cheaply. It began arriving at Nagasaki on junks from Zhapu, and within a year or two it was all over the print shops of Edo.

great-wave-1830.label: The Great Wave
great-wave-1830.title: Under the Wave off Kanagawa
great-wave-1830.text: Hokusai’s print of a wave about to fall on three boats, with Mount Fuji small in the distance. It was one of the first prints made in the new, cheap Prussian blue.

faraday-1831.label: Faraday's generator
faraday-1831.title: A magnet and a coil of wire
faraday-1831.text: Michael Faraday pushed a magnet into a coil of wire and made electricity flow in it. Nearly every power station in the world works that way now.

daumier-gargantua-1831.label: Daumier draws the king
daumier-gargantua-1831.title: Six months for a drawing
daumier-gargantua-1831.text: In December 1831 Honoré Daumier published a drawing of the king of France as a giant on a throne, being fed baskets of money carried up a plank by the poor. He was fined and sentenced to six months in prison.

beagle-1831.label: The Beagle sails
beagle-1831.title: Five years round the world
beagle-1831.text: HMS Beagle left Plymouth at the end of December 1831 to chart the coasts of South America, with a young Charles Darwin on board. It came home nearly five years later.

hiroshige-tokaido-1833.label: Hiroshige’s road to Kyoto
hiroshige-tokaido-1833.title: Fifty-three stations
hiroshige-tokaido-1833.text: Utagawa Hiroshige published prints of the fifty-three stopping places on the great road from Edo to Kyoto. They were a great success.

stereoscope-1838.label: Wheatstone’s stereoscope
stereoscope-1838.title: Two flat drawings, one solid
stereoscope-1838.text: Charles Wheatstone showed that each eye sees a slightly different picture. Give each eye its own flat drawing, through a pair of mirrors, and the two become one solid thing standing in front of you.

photography-1839.label: First photos
photography-1839.title: A picture nobody drew
photography-1839.text: In January 1839 Louis Daguerre’s way of fixing a picture made by light was announced in Paris. For the first time a picture could be made without anybody drawing it.

perry-1853.label: US warships in Edo Bay
perry-1853.title: The door comes open
perry-1853.text: In July 1853 four American warships, two of them driven by steam, anchored at the mouth of Edo Bay and would not leave. The next year Japan signed a treaty with the United States, and the door began to open.

origin-of-species-1859.label: Origin of Species
origin-of-species-1859.title: Twenty years of putting it off
origin-of-species-1859.text: Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species in London in November 1859, twenty years after he first wrote the idea down for himself. Booksellers took the whole first printing on the day it appeared.

edison-lamp-1879.label: Edison's lightbulb
edison-lamp-1879.title: Light without fire
edison-lamp-1879.text: In October 1879 Thomas Edison's workshop ran a glass bulb with a thread of carbon inside it for more than half a day. Within three years there were streets lit by electricity in New York and London.

eiffel-tower-1889.label: Eiffel Tower
eiffel-tower-1889.title: The tallest thing anyone had built
eiffel-tower-1889.text: Three hundred metres of iron went up in Paris in two years and opened to the public on 15 May 1889, in the middle of a world's fair. At night ten thousand gas lamps picked out its shape, and a beacon burned under a glass dome at the top.
